question_text: What were the main causes and consequences of the 1857 revolt against British rule in India?
correct_answer: Causes: use of greased cartridges (Enfield rifle), rapid annexation of princely states under Doctrine of Lapse, economic exploitation through deindustrialization of Indian industries, social interference through widow remarriage act and Christian missionary activities, and resentment of Indian sepoys at unequal treatment. Consequences: end of East India Company rule, Crown took direct control (Queen's Proclamation 1858), creation of Indian Civil Service, British policy became cautious about social reform.
key_points: Enfield rifle cartridges as immediate trigger
Doctrine of Lapse caused widespread resentment among rulers
End of East India Company — direct Crown rule 1858
Queen's Proclamation promised non-interference in Indian customs
tip: Connect immediate military cause to deeper economic and political causes — show analytical depth.

question_text: Explain the Partition of Bengal in 1905 and its impact on Indian nationalism.
correct_answer: Lord Curzon partitioned Bengal in 1905 into East Bengal (Muslim majority) and West Bengal (Hindu majority) citing administrative convenience. Nationalists saw it as a deliberate divide-and-rule strategy. The Swadeshi Movement emerged as a response — boycott of British goods, promotion of indigenous products. Led to formation of All India Muslim League in 1906. Partition was annulled in 1911 due to massive protests. It radicalized Indian nationalism and gave birth to mass politics.
key_points: 1905: Curzon divides Bengal on religious lines
Swadeshi and Boycott movements as response
Muslim League formed 1906 in Dhaka
Partition annulled 1911 — British capitulation to mass protest
tip: Partition of Bengal is the turning point from moderate to radical nationalism — explain this evolution.

question_text: What was the significance of the Gandhi-Irwin Pact of 1931?
correct_answer: The Gandhi-Irwin Pact (March 1931) ended the Civil Disobedience Movement temporarily. Key terms: British agreed to release political prisoners, restore confiscated properties of satyagrahis, allow salt making near the sea coast, and allow peaceful picketing. Congress agreed to attend Second Round Table Conference and suspend the movement. Significance: British officially recognized Congress as legitimate representative body, Gandhi represented Congress at Round Table Conference.
key_points: Ended Civil Disobedience Movement temporarily
Gandhi to attend Second Round Table Conference
British recognized Congress as legitimate voice
Release of political prisoners and confiscated property
tip: Pact was controversial — many nationalists felt Gandhi made too many concessions. Know the criticism.

question_text: Describe the economic impact of British rule on India's agricultural sector.
correct_answer: British rule transformed Indian agriculture in damaging ways. Introduction of Permanent Settlement (1793) in Bengal created a class of absentee zamindars who extracted maximum rent without investing in land. Ryotwari system in Madras placed excessive tax burden directly on farmers. Introduction of cash crops (cotton, indigo, jute) for export at expense of food crops caused famines. De-industrialization forced artisans back to agriculture, increasing pressure on land. Result: recurring famines, peasant indebtedness, and rural poverty.
key_points: Permanent Settlement created exploitative zamindari class
Cash crops over food crops caused food insecurity
De-industrialization increased pressure on agriculture
Deindustrialization + land revenue = recurring famines
tip: Connect Permanent Settlement to the Great Bengal Famine of 1943 — long-term structural damage.

question_text: What were the key provisions of the Indian Independence Act of 1947?
correct_answer: The Indian Independence Act (July 1947) partitioned British India into two independent dominions — India and Pakistan. Key provisions: British India divided from 15 August 1947, princely states free to join either dominion or remain independent, both dominions to have Governor-General, British Parliament's authority over India ended, Indian legislature given full legislative powers, and Constituent Assemblies to frame constitutions. It transferred power but left partition borders (Radcliffe Line) to be announced after independence.
key_points: 15 August 1947 partition into India and Pakistan
Princely states given choice — accession not mandatory
Both dominions: dominion status under British Crown initially
Radcliffe Line demarcated borders — announced after independence
tip: Cyril Radcliffe announced borders on 17 August — two days after independence, causing maximum confusion.

question_text: Explain the Jallianwala Bagh massacre and its political consequences.
correct_answer: On 13 April 1919 (Baisakhi), General Dyer ordered troops to fire on a peaceful gathering of unarmed civilians (including women and children) protesting the Rowlatt Act at Jallianwala Bagh, Amritsar. Exits were blocked. Official count: 379 killed, thousands wounded. Actual estimates higher. Consequences: Rabindranath Tagore returned his knighthood, national outrage transformed moderate into militant nationalists, Gandhi organized Non-Cooperation Movement (1920), and permanently damaged British moral legitimacy in India.
key_points: 13 April 1919, Amritsar — General Dyer ordered unprovoked firing
Protest against Rowlatt Act (arrest without trial)
Tagore returned knighthood as protest
Directly led to Non-Cooperation Movement 1920
tip: Hunter Commission report was weak — British failure to punish Dyer exposed racial double standards.

question_text: What were the main features of the Maurya Empire under Chandragupta Maurya and Ashoka?
correct_answer: Chandragupta Maurya (322-298 BCE) founded the empire with help of Chanakya, defeated Nanda dynasty, unified most of the subcontinent. Arthashastra described centralized bureaucracy with a spy network. Ashoka (268-232 BCE) expanded the empire to its peak, then renounced violence after Kalinga War (261 BCE). Spread Buddhism through dhamma, sent missionaries to Sri Lanka, sent Dhamma edicts on rocks and pillars. Centralized administration with provinces (rashtras) governed by princes or governors.
key_points: Chandragupta unified India with Chanakya's guidance
Arthashastra: first systematic text on statecraft and economics
Kalinga War (261 BCE) turned Ashoka to Buddhism
Ashoka's edicts — earliest evidence of governance philosophy in India
tip: Megasthenes (Greek ambassador) wrote Indica about Chandragupta's court — use as corroborating source.

question_text: What was the significance of the Non-Cooperation Movement (1920-22)?
correct_answer: Non-Cooperation Movement (1920-1922) was Gandhi's first mass movement. Indians were asked to return British titles, boycott government schools and courts, boycott foreign cloth and use khadi, boycott legislative councils, and not join the army. Mass participation transformed Congress from elite to mass organization. Called off after Chauri Chaura incident (1922) where mob burned police station killing 22 policemen. Critics: abrupt withdrawal demoralized nationalists. Significance: first time all sections of society participated.
key_points: First truly mass movement — peasants, workers, students all participated
Return of titles, boycott of schools, courts, foreign goods
Chauri Chaura (Feb 1922) — Gandhi called off movement
Transformed Congress from elite club to mass organization
tip: Chauri Chaura as turning point — Gandhi's insistence on non-violence was controversial but principled.

question_text: Explain the Poona Pact (1932) and its significance for Dalit representation.
correct_answer: The Communal Award (1932) by British PM Ramsay MacDonald proposed separate electorates for Depressed Classes (Dalits). Ambedkar supported this as it would ensure Dalit political representation. Gandhi fasted unto death opposing separate electorates, arguing it would permanently divide Hindu society. The Poona Pact (September 1932) was a compromise: separate electorates abandoned, but reserved seats for Depressed Classes increased from 71 to 148 in provincial legislatures with joint electorate.
key_points: Communal Award proposed separate electorates for Dalits
Gandhi fasted against it — Ambedkar supported separate electorates
Poona Pact compromise: reserved seats in joint electorate
Long-standing debate: who compromised more — Gandhi or Ambedkar
tip: Know the Ambedkar-Gandhi conflict on this — it remains relevant to debates on reservations today.

question_text: What was the Indus Valley Civilization and what evidence suggests its advanced urban planning?
correct_answer: The Indus Valley Civilization (2600-1900 BCE) was one of the world's earliest urban civilizations, covering present-day Pakistan and northwestern India. Key sites: Harappa, Mohenjo-daro, Lothal (Gujarat), Dholavira (Gujarat). Evidence of urban planning: grid-pattern street layout, covered drainage system superior to many modern cities, standardized brick sizes, dedicated granaries, public baths (Great Bath at Mohenjo-daro), and a script not yet fully deciphered.
key_points: 2600-1900 BCE, spread across Pakistan and NW India
Grid streets and covered drainage system
Standardized weights and measures — trade network
No evidence of large palaces or kings — possibly merchant republics
tip: Contrast with Mesopotamia and Egypt — IVC cities show less evidence of rulers/religion, more civic planning.

question_text: What were the causes and outcomes of the Third Battle of Panipat (1761)?
correct_answer: The Third Battle of Panipat (January 1761) was fought between the Maratha Empire and Ahmad Shah Durrani (Afghanistan). Causes: Durrani invading to restore Mughal power and counter Maratha expansion northward. The Marathas, led by Vishwasrao and Bhau Saheb, faced logistical failures — long supply lines from Pune to Delhi weakened their army. Outcome: decisive Durrani victory, massive Maratha loss of over 100,000 men. It halted Maratha expansion and created a power vacuum exploited by the British.
key_points: January 1761: Ahmad Shah Durrani vs Marathas
Maratha supply line failure — decisive factor
Massive Maratha losses — political recovery took decades
Created power vacuum — British exploitation followed
tip: Connect battle outcome to British rise — no other Indian power could fill the Maratha void.

question_text: Explain the significance of the Quit India Movement (1942).
correct_answer: The Quit India Movement (August 1942) was Gandhi's final mass movement demanding immediate independence. 'Do or Die' was the rallying cry. British arrested all major leaders within 24 hours, forcing leaderless mass uprising — parallel government established in some areas. Brutal British suppression with 100,000 arrests, police firings. Significance: demonstrated British inability to govern India with popular consent, accelerated post-war independence talks, and showed resolve of the Indian people. Though militarily unsuccessful, politically decisive.
key_points: August 8, 1942 — 'Do or Die' resolution
British arrested all leaders immediately
Underground movement, parallel governments in some areas
Proved India ungovernable against popular will — accelerated 1947
tip: Aruna Asaf Ali hoisted the Congress flag at Gowalia Tank — symbol of defiance when leaders arrested.

question_text: What were the key reforms introduced by the Government of India Act 1919?
correct_answer: Government of India Act 1919 (Montague-Chelmsford Reforms) introduced dyarchy in provinces — subjects divided into transferred (education, health — Indian ministers responsible) and reserved (finance, law — British controlled). Bicameral legislature at centre (Council of State and Legislative Assembly) with limited powers. Expanded franchise based on property ownership. Communal electorates for Muslims confirmed. Separate electorates for Sikhs added. Indians got some real power at provincial level for the first time.
key_points: Dyarchy: transferred subjects to Indian ministers, reserved to British
Bicameral central legislature — still limited powers
Expanded franchise — property based
Failed to satisfy nationalist demands — too little too late
tip: Dyarchy was criticized as unworkable — responsible for some functions but not for finance needed to run them.
